deck.section_name: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry
deck.title: Covalent Bonding & Structure

front_blocks.md: What is a polar covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A **polar covalent bond** forms when two atoms of different electronegativities share electrons. The more electronegative atom draws the electrons toward itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ−), while the less electronegative atom gains a partial positive charge (δ+).

cards.front_md: What is a polar covalent bond?
cards.back_md: A **polar covalent bond** forms when two atoms of different electronegativities share electrons. The more electronegative atom draws the electrons toward itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ−), while the less electronegative atom gains a partial positive charge (δ+).

front_blocks.md: Define **covalent bond**

back_blocks.md: A **covalent bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two non-metal atoms and the pair of electrons they share. No electrons are transferred; instead, two atomic orbitals overlap to form a molecular orbital.

cards.front_md: Define **covalent bond**
cards.back_md: A **covalent bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two non-metal atoms and the pair of electrons they share. No electrons are transferred; instead, two atomic orbitals overlap to form a molecular orbital.

front_blocks.md: Why are electrons shared in a covalent bond rather than remaining with one atom?

back_blocks.md: Electrons are more stable when attracted to **two nuclei** simultaneously. Sharing electrons allows each atom to achieve a full outer shell similar to a **noble gas** configuration, lowering the overall energy of the system.

cards.front_md: Why are electrons shared in a covalent bond rather than remaining with one atom?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Electrons are transferred between atoms during covalent bond formation.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In covalent bonding, electrons are **shared** between atoms, not transferred. Both atoms contribute electrons to the shared pair, and neither atom permanently loses electrons.

front_blocks.md: Why do simple covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points?

back_blocks.md: Simple covalent molecules are held together by **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules. Only a little energy is needed to overcome these forces and separate the molecules, so melting and boiling points are low.

front_blocks.md: Why do simple covalent compounds not conduct electricity in the solid or liquid state?

back_blocks.md: Simple covalent compounds contain no **charged particles** (ions or free electrons) in the solid or liquid state. Without mobile charge carriers, there is no mechanism for electrical conduction.

front_blocks.md: Why do giant covalent structures have very high melting and boiling points?

back_blocks.md: Giant covalent structures contain a huge number of **strong covalent bonds** linking atoms throughout the whole lattice. A very large amount of energy is required to break enough of these bonds to melt or boil the substance.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

In graphite, each carbon atom forms three bonds, leaving one **delocalised electron** per atom free to carry charge. In diamond, all four outer electrons on each carbon atom form covalent bonds, leaving no free electrons.

front_blocks.md: Why is BF<sub>3</sub> described as electron deficient?

back_blocks.md: In BF<sub>3</sub>, boron has only three outer electrons and forms three covalent bonds. This gives boron only **6 electrons** around it in the molecule, fewer than the 8 required to complete a full octet.

front_blocks.md: Define **dative covalent bond**

back_blocks.md: A **dative covalent bond** (also called a coordinate bond) is a covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom. The donor atom provides a lone pair to an electron-deficient acceptor atom.

front_blocks.md: What two conditions are needed for a dative covalent bond to form?

back_blocks.md: One atom must have a **lone pair** of electrons available to donate, and the other atom must be **electron-deficient**, having an unfilled outer orbital that can accept the lone pair.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In a dative covalent bond, **both electrons** come from the **same atom** (the donor). This distinguishes it from an ordinary covalent bond where each atom contributes one electron.

front_blocks.md: Why does the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) contain a dative covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: When NH<sub>3</sub> reacts with H<sup>+</sup>, nitrogen donates its **lone pair** to the electron-deficient proton. The H<sup>+</sup> has an empty shell and accepts the pair, forming a **dative covalent bond** and giving the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion all four equivalent N-H bonds.

front_blocks.md: How does the number of shared electron pairs differ between a single, double and triple covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A **single bond** contains 1 shared pair of electrons, a **double bond** contains 2 shared pairs and a **triple bond** contains 3 shared pairs. More shared pairs result in a shorter and stronger bond.

front_blocks.md: What are the key conventions when drawing a covalent dot-and-cross diagram?

back_blocks.md: Only **outer-shell (valence) electrons** are shown. Dots represent electrons from one atom and crosses from the other. Shared pairs are drawn in the overlap between the two atoms, and lone pairs are shown on the outside of each atom.

front_blocks.md: Define **allotrope**

back_blocks.md: An **allotrope** is one of two or more different physical forms of the same element, arising from different bonding arrangements of its atoms. For example, diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon.

front_blocks.md: Why is graphite soft and slippery?

back_blocks.md: In graphite, the layers of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms are held together only by **weak van der Waals' forces**. These forces are easily overcome, allowing the layers to slide over each other.

front_blocks.md: Why does graphite conduct electricity?

back_blocks.md: Each carbon atom in graphite bonds to only three others, leaving one **delocalised electron** per carbon atom. These delocalised electrons can move along the layers and carry charge when a voltage is applied.

Diamond conducts electricity.

front_blocks.md: Why is diamond one of the hardest known substances?

back_blocks.md: In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to **four** others via strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network. Breaking this structure requires overcoming a very large number of strong bonds simultaneously.

back_blocks.md: **Electronegativity** is the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It is measured on the Pauling scale, with fluorine having the highest value of 4.0.

front_blocks.md: How does the difference in electronegativity between two atoms determine the type of bond formed?

back_blocks.md: A difference of **2 or more** on the Pauling scale leads to an **ionic bond**. A difference of **less than 2** leads to a **covalent bond**, with greater polarity as the difference increases toward 2.

front_blocks.md: What is a nonpolar covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A **nonpolar covalent bond** exists when two atoms with the **same electronegativity** share electrons equally. The electron distribution is symmetric and there are no partial charges on either atom.

front_blocks.md: Why is CH<sub>3</sub>Cl a polar molecule but CCl<sub>4</sub> is not, even though both contain polar C-Cl bonds?

back_blocks.md: In CCl<sub>4</sub> the four C-Cl dipoles are arranged **symmetrically** and cancel out, giving a net dipole of zero. In CH<sub>3</sub>Cl the four different bonds are arranged **asymmetrically**, so the dipoles do not cancel and the molecule has an overall **dipole moment**.

front_blocks.md: What is **VSEPR theory**?

back_blocks.md: **VSEPR theory** (valence shell electron pair repulsion theory) predicts the shape and bond angles of molecules. It states that electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to minimise these repulsions.

front_blocks.md: How does increasing bond order (from single to double to triple) affect bond length and strength?

back_blocks.md: As bond order increases, **bond length decreases** and **bond strength increases**. Greater electron density between the nuclei increases the attractive forces, pulling the atoms closer together and making the bond harder to break.

back_blocks.md: NH<sub>3</sub> is a **trigonal pyramid** with bond angles of **107°**. Nitrogen has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pair exerts greater repulsion than a bonding pair, compressing the H-N-H angles below the 109.5° of CH<sub>4</sub>.
